text:
Chapter Seventeen


Before Arthur’s Materials Alchemy class, Rory had lectured him in a series of texts that were rattling around in Arthur’s brain as he walked into the courtyard.




Rory Farrell: What do you mean nothing has worked? What have you tried?






Rory Farrell: We came up with this plan a week ago






Arthur: I feel like it’s important to put in writing that you came up with this plan






Rory Farrell: You don’t have to make out with her in the middle of campus, just do something






Rory Farrell: Talk to her, get close to her, do what you did that night!




It wasn’t worth explaining to Rory all the things he’d tried, but when he looked up at Maggie with that guarded grin on her face and saw the hawthorn petals that were stuck in her hair, he had the half thought that it must be divine intervention.


“Hi, Maggie,” he said when he was close enough to reach out and brush them away. His voice was quiet as he brought his hand up to her hair, letting his fingers graze her earlobe as he did it. He tried not to look like he was searching her expression for some sort of recognition, so he kept talking. “You should have come in and joined us, shown off your materials knowledge.”


If there was anything in Maggie’s expression as he pulled his hand away, it was relief as the petal blew away on the wind. “You know very well I haven’t taken that class in over thirteen years. Your students would put me to shame.”


Arthur shrugged. “I think you probably have many talents I don’t know about.”


Even in the dreary light, Arthur could make out the blush that bloomed on Maggie’s face. He wanted to reach out again and brush her skin, feel the heat in her cheeks. But he didn’t, of course. No matter how much he wanted to. No matter how proud Rory would be.


Maggie cleared her throat. “Dr. Paige is waiting for us.” They walked through the archway that led from the courtyard to the covered pathway connecting Ilex Hall with the rest of campus. When the grounds came into view, Arthur was pleased to see the grow lights dotting the landscape, nestled into flower beds and hanging from tree branches to combat the hazy gloom produced by the pall. Maggie seemed to forget their awkward moment when she saw them, her face brightening. “I hate that we need them,” Maggie said, “but maybe this one small thing isn’t so terrible.”


A groundskeeper had crafted the clever lights, and Dean Clearwater had shown Arthur the plan earlier in the week. It had been such a relief to have one less thing eating away at him, especially after he persuaded Dean Clearwater to talk to the administration about providing the lights to local residents. “The school is going to distribute free lights to anyone within a mile radius who needs them. Hopefully it will stave off some of the ecological impacts of this cloud cover,” he said. “Maybe you could take a couple home for your balcony?”


They stepped off the main campus walkway to a winding brick pathway that snaked up the hill toward the edge of campus. Other than Ilex Hall, there were six other buildings on campus, some that were original to the property and some that were built as it transitioned to a college over the past century. The historical center was in the Annex, one of the original buildings. It came into view as they followed the path around Ferox Hall.


The squat building was made out of silver shale stone and covered in moss and lichen. It had an original thatched roof that must need to be rethatched every few years, and it was surrounded by a copse of trees, nearly reclaimed by the Wilds. It looked like one of the faerie cottages from the old Diadhan poems that Maggie loved so much.


Inside, it felt like someone’s home instead of a university building. In one room, original furniture—fussy things covered in ornate, lush fabrics and tall, glistening wood cabinets—was arranged as it had been when this was a guesthouse for the main manor. Arthur felt like he had walked into someone’s grandmother’s house. Someone’s very rich grandmother, anyway.


They stood in the small entryway, idly looking at the antiques, when a small blond woman wearing a pantsuit came down the crooked staircase at the back of the cottage. Arthur had gotten so bad at telling how old anyone was, but she seemed a little bit younger than him and Maggie. “Welcome to the Annex,” she said. “I’m Pearl Paige.”


“Thank you so much for meeting us on short notice, Dr. Paige.” Arthur held out a hand for her to shake.


“Please, Pearl is fine.” Arthur noticed the slight blush on her cheeks as she talked to him, but he ignored it, even as she stumbled over her words slightly. He may be Artie among his family and his brother’s friends, but for most of his life, he had been Rowena Taliesin’s son. And then, in the last five years, people had started to get nervous around him for his own sake as he built a name and reputation for himself in the alchemy world. It didn’t matter that it had been happening for as long as he could remember, it still made him uncomfortable.


“This is Dr. Maggie Linden,” Arthur said, to give Pearl something and someone else to focus on. Thankfully, it worked. Dr. Paige visibly calmed talking to Maggie.


“I teach in the Linguistics and Incantation Translation Department.” Hawthorn was a small campus, but it wasn’t so small that they knew every professor or researcher who worked there. “It’s been so long since I came over to the Annex,” Maggie said, and Arthur suspected she was trying to put Dr. Paige at ease. “I think the last time I was here was when I first started, but that was when your predecessor worked here. Dr. Milliner?”


Dr. Paige nodded in recognition and then settled into a well-rehearsed speech explaining how the Annex functioned as a repository of all things Hawthorn history. It housed information on the original owners of the manor house from more than a century ago and on the transition of the property from private residence to public college. The modern records in the building were about Hawthorn’s integral role in the local community in the present day.


“While our antiques often entice visitors”—Dr. Paige mentioned offhand, and Arthur’s gaze darted to Maggie, who seemed to be waiting for him with arched brows as if to say, Who is coming to look at these dusty old things? He hid a grin behind his hand as Dr. Paige went on—“the main draw is our collection of antique maps and information about Galloway and the Wilds. We serve as a historical record for the town, too.”


She led them out of the main room, with its stuffy furniture, to a wide room off to the side. This one was bright and had been modernized, unlike other parts of the house. Instead of smelling like dust, it had the faint scent of disinfectant and paper. Large metal flat files that went from floor to ceiling lined the walls, along with stacks of filing and storage cabinets. Dr. Paige tugged her key off her neck, the retractable wire making a zipping sound, and unlocked two of the cases nearest to them. She slid open one of the drawers, revealing rows of documents in neat folders. On her other side, she opened one of the flat files at hip level to reveal a yellowing stack of papers as wide and long as a table. Arthur could just make out topographical notations on the top one.


“The documents are organized chronologically,” Dr. Paige went on, patting her hand on the wide drawer. “We have records going back about two hundred years, but the vast majority are from about fifty years before the manor was built and onward.” She gestured to filing cabinets on the other side of a long table in the middle of the room. “Those cabinets over there contain hard copies of periodicals and newspapers, but we also have those recorded on microfiche.” She gestured to a particularly ancient-looking, dusty machine and then squat cabinets in the corner of the room, where the ceiling started to slope downward. “Those cabinets have town records—deeds, election ballots, that sort of thing—organized by decade.”


“This is an impressive collection,” Maggie said, picking up a corner of the map in the flat file and looking at the one beneath it. Maggie was right. There had to be something here that could help them uncover what was feeding the pall.


“Yes, it was imperative to the first president of the university that the school’s history was preserved, along with its connection to Galloway,” Dr. Paige explained. “We’re fully staffed by university librarians who float between the Annex and the library throughout the school year. But, as you know, we’re closing up shop for the summer in a few days, so I’m very happy we could squeeze you in.”


“We really appreciate it.” Maggie looked eagerly at the document cases.


“Is there anything in particular I can help you find?”


Arthur walked around the room, dropping his head slightly to avoid the sloping roof. “Where would I find information about the original surveys done on the land, from before the manor house was even built? We’re hoping to find maps of the Wilds over time, too.”


She patted the cabinet on her right. “The earliest records are in this cabinet here. You should find the early survey work, and I know there are diaries from naturalists who documented the Wilds in there.”


With a quick goodbye, and a reminder about proper document handling, she left them with a key and a promise to return in an hour or so to check on them. Maggie immediately descended on the drawers, carefully pulling out old survey maps and laying them gingerly on the table in the center of the room. Arthur chose to read through one of the journals, this one from a naturalist who explored the Wilds about a decade before the manor house was built.


For a while, they pored over the documents in silence, the only sound between them the shuffling of pages being turned or the scratch of pen across paper. Arthur liked this quiet work, side by side. He liked that Maggie didn’t feel like she had to talk to fill the air around them. He liked when their silences weren’t awkward, only content.


He wished that they didn’t have to be trapped in some kind of bargain to make it happen. He wished he were brave enough to take the mask swinging from her rearview mirror as a sign that Beltane had affected her as much as him. But he had convinced himself that she wouldn’t feel the same when she realized it was him, couldn’t imagine that she would want to work with him closely after she found out.


He realized he had read the same page a half dozen times when Maggie’s clear voice cut through the silence and the prattle in Arthur’s brain. “Take a look at this.”


He walked over, leaning close until he could smell her shampoo. She was looking at a map of the Wilds and the yet-unincorporated town of Galloway when it was just a frequently traveled trail for horses and a couple of stables. “About thirty years before they built the original Hawthorn manor house, they attempted to build a road through the Wilds.” The map showed the proposed road, a straight line through the Wilds to the marshland on the other side. “The road would connect with a ferry station, giving more direct access to Atlantia instead of having to go all the way around the Wilds to get there.


“As far as I can see, they’ve attempted to build this road no less than six times since.” She pointed to reference files connected to the maps she looked at. “Every time, the construction sites are overrun by fantasmia, the trees don’t stay still, and the very land itself seems to rebel against the idea that it can be tamed. We already know that fantasmia activity within the Wilds is higher than the rest of this part of the country. What if it’s some sort of feedback loop? The presence of all those ghouls and wraiths creating energy that feeds the pall.”


Arthur thought for a moment. “That could be contributing, but if it were just that, don’t you think there would have been palls like this in the past?” He paused again, chewing on his lip as he thought. “Why are there more fantasmia in the Wilds? Why are the Wilds so strange to begin with?”


Maggie sighed in frustration and returned to her research, while Arthur had entirely too difficult a time pulling himself away from the smell of her hair. When he finally managed it, the scent lingered. Lavender. He probably wouldn’t have recognized it a week ago, but now it was burned into his memory. He had felt hypnotized as he had rolled that lavender candy over his tongue—he thought it tasted like a candle, and it definitely did nothing to calm down the way he felt when he looked at Maggie’s lips.


Gods below, focus. He opened the journal, found the passage he had already read three or four times, and started again. The naturalist, a man by the name of Wheatly, was diagramming a strange vine that grew in the Wilds that was only found climbing the pale mottled bark of the river birch. River birches were plentiful even among the Wilds’ more common pines because of the three rivers that coursed through the forest. Three rivers that converged into one…


“Maggie,” he said, breathless, and she was next to him in an instant. “What if there was a convergence?”


She scrunched up her nose. “The odds…”


“I think we are working well outside the realm of likely already.”


She pulled out her phone, opening an astrological app, dismissing with a huff a horoscope that he only just caught a glimpse of. Open yourself to possibilities of…


“Well, damn,” she said, turning the phone so he could get a better look. On May 6, the day the pall fell, there had been a lunar conjunction—the moon and two planets, appearing all in a line in the sky. It had lasted approximately thirty-six hours, with its peak for the latitude and longitude of the Wilds and Hawthorn College landing right at…“Three fifty-four p.m.,” Maggie said, her voice heavy with disbelief.


“A conjunction of three planetary bodies above a confluence of three rivers.” Arthur sighed, drawing his finger along the map in front of Maggie. She leaned over him to get a better look at the map, seeming to not even notice the way her breasts pressed against his arm. It nearly sent him into a tailspin as quickly as the unlucky—and unlikely—news that there had been a convergence. The power of three invoked on the earth or sky twice over.


Arthur’s mind was spinning. Earth magic—the way earthly and heavenly constructs affected magic—was one of the earliest and least understood branches of magic. If all spells were conduits for energy, pulling it from one place and putting it somewhere else, convergences were fonts of energy that could easily supercharge a spell—or a mistake.


“Anything else come in threes that day?” Maggie asked, scanning the map. There was a hard edge to her voice that hadn’t been there a moment ago.


“Wasn’t that enough?” he groaned. “I swear, this kind of luck…”


Maggie glared at him over her shoulder, still not doing anything about how close they were. “Was it luck? Or being unprepared?” she snapped, her face inches from his. Arthur felt like he couldn’t breathe. “Didn’t you think to check the astrological forecast?”


“Do you check the astrological forecast before every spell you cast?” he retorted, knowing very well she didn’t. It was a good practice, but an unfavorable astrological transit alone couldn’t set off a pall. It wasn’t just the planetary conjunction fueling the pall, but its presence directly over the river confluence at the exact time of his mistake.


Her anger made the air feel charged. He wanted to risk electrocution and close the space between them so he could press his lips against hers until she forgot about the mess he’d made.


“I wasn’t doing any class three alchemical spells in front of students!” Something had changed in her expression, a shift from an anger that burned like heat to one that doused him with ice water. “I’m sure your colleagues in the Astrology Department will be thrilled with this revelation.” She laughed, but there was no humor in it, and shook her head. “You clearly value their work as much as you value mine.”


Arthur didn’t understand what she meant. When had he ever given her reason to believe he didn’t value her work? He knew she thought he was a screwup, but the strength of her anger didn’t make any sense to him. Whatever spell had drawn them closer was well and truly broken as Maggie turned away. The silence was no longer comfortable but instead threaded with tension. He wanted to puzzle over what she had said, about the obvious untruth of it, but they had only one afternoon in the Annex.


The guilt and shame he felt about the pall settled in his stomach like a rock. Maggie seemed to have suspected that he failed in some way long before they started working together, and now here was the proof. He clenched his jaw.


The focus of their research shifted to ensuring there wasn’t another element to this convergence, and they pored over the books, maps, and documents for the rest of their hour, interrupted only once by a confused Dr. Paige. Even she could feel the way the air was thick with everything unsaid between them.


“There’s nothing else here,” Maggie finally said, after another hour of work. She dropped a book onto the table with a final thud. “Nothing obvious, anyway.”


She started shuffling papers and putting them away, each movement punctuated by frustration. He was afraid she was going to run off before he could make this right, before he could make her understand exactly how brilliant he thought she was, but he didn’t want to talk to her in here. Not where Dr. Paige could interrupt them at any minute, so he endured the tortured silence a little longer.



—


Maggie wasn’t being fair, and she knew it. Somehow, every complicated feeling she had for Taliesin was being reduced to a decoction of uncomplicated anger, and she had a horoscope to blame.


When Dr. Paige had left them, they had slipped into their still-new rhythm that felt too familiar and too easy, so different from the first weeks they shared an office. She was still aware of every one of Taliesin’s movements, but she found her heart racing for a completely different reason. It was so much easier when he was infuriating her. And then, as she’d opened her planetary transit app to confirm the conjunction, the horoscope had flashed across her screen: This is the season to open yourself to the possibility of love in unlikely places.


Now the damn stars were pushing her toward Taliesin, too? She was mad at herself for even thinking it—love? Taliesin? This was…well, she didn’t know what it was, but it wasn’t that. They didn’t even like each other. Not really. It would be easier to look for the masked man from Beltane, easier to find a stranger she couldn’t even recognize than entertain whatever made working beside Taliesin feel so comfortable. Easy. The way working with her ex, Evan, had once felt easy before he betrayed her. She slid the notification away with so much force, she knew he noticed it with that observant gaze that was always searching her for something.


She was scrambling to find purchase, to put herself squarely somewhere safe and comfortable. So she picked the fight. Selfish Taliesin, arrogant Taliesin, was familiar territory. Better than the man who looked at her with heat in his eyes, who cared for his students, who was good at his job.


It didn’t matter that her argument was thin, that he was right when he asked her if she checked astrological transits before every spell she cast. Of course she didn’t. Plus, she had been working at Hawthorn for four years to Taliesin’s nine months, and she had never once considered the three rivers running through the Wilds as a possible convergence point just waiting for another naturally occurring power of three to cause havoc. The odds of a convergence, of a spell being cast and a potent mistake setting off a chain reaction at the exact moment the planets were square above the confluence of the river, was so unlikely…unlucky, his word that she had such a problem with, really was the right description.


But even as she could rationally agree with him, her brain worked overtime to sabotage whatever was pulling their bodies closer and closer together. He could pretend to be kind and open when it suited him, but at the end of the day, all she really knew about him was what he did. What he did was dismiss her and her work by slashing her budget. What he did was ignore the importance of an astrological transit on his class 3 spell and then have the nerve to call it luck.


When they left the Annex, saying awkward have a good summers to Dr. Paige, Maggie tried to walk out ahead of him, forgetting for a moment that their destination was one and the same and Taliesin’s legs were significantly longer than hers. He didn’t say anything, but he did keep up, the tension between them coiling tighter and tighter as they returned to Ilex Hall.


Back in their office, she dropped a book Dr. Paige had given her on Galloway history onto her desk when Taliesin had finally had enough. “What did I say to upset you?”


Maggie scoffed. She tried to keep the sound to herself, tried to keep it in her head, but of course it didn’t work out that way. “Forget it,” she said. She didn’t want to have this conversation, not now. She needed to go home and cool down so they could get through this summer working together. “Don’t worry about it.”


“Of course I’m going to worry about it,” he said, exasperated. Maggie understood—she was sick of herself, too—but she couldn’t bring herself to stop. She glanced up from the spot on her desk that she had been studying intently. He had spun his desk chair around, and his hand was curled in a tight fist on his knee. His brow was furrowed, and he looked at her like she was a mystery that needed to be solved, which only ignited another spark of indignation in her.


“Fine, you want to know what you did? You’re arrogant…”


“A jerk. Rude. Inconsiderate,” he said, looking wounded and sounding like he was reciting something. “I know, Maggie. I heard you that day in Dahlia and Jim’s office.” Her stomach coiled with something like shame. “I know you don’t like me very much. But what is this about?”


“You can’t go around acting like your field of research is the only one that matters. People care what you think here,” she said. I care what you think, her traitorous mind supplied, but she managed to keep that to herself. She took a shallow breath, ignoring the burning pinpricks of tears in her eyes.


“What have I ever done to make you think I don’t value your work?” he asked as he ran his fingers through his hair. When she didn’t answer him right away, he went on. “I don’t know what you’re talking about.”


“That’s the problem!” she yelled. “You came to Hawthorn because you needed to get away from your life at Dartwood, and, believe me, I get it. But getting stupid committee assignments is part of the territory at a small college.” Gods below, she was rambling. None of this was coming out right, and she was afraid she was going to start crying any minute. “Did you really think that I wouldn’t notice?” His furrow deepened. “Eight thousand dollars from my budget isn’t a percentage; it’s the entire thing.”


“What did I do?” His voice had a desperate edge to it that she, frustratingly, wanted to smooth away. “I can’t fix it if I don’t know what I did.”


She sighed, rubbing away a tear before it could fall. “I run a translation seminar every fall semester for fourth-year students who are considering academic careers. It’s a graduate-level class, and it involves a field-study trip at the beginning of the semester that the students base their research on. Without the field study, I’d have to restructure the entire seminar. Which I absolutely didn’t have time to do this year. So, when I found out my budget was cut, next year’s class was canceled. Done. When I checked the budget committee’s recommendations, guess who signed off on the cut?”


Arthur closed his eyes and sat back. “Mine.”


“Yours.”


He looked exhausted in the pale light filtering through her tiny window. “Why didn’t you say something sooner?” he asked quietly.


The tears Maggie had been trying so hard to avoid welled up, and with them, more frustration and anger. “Because every time I would think about talking to you about it”—she gestured toward her face—“this would happen.”


She turned away, angling her chair so she was facing her computer, and hiccuped as she brushed away the tears that fell down her cheeks. She knew she probably looked mottled and blotchy, but she didn’t care. She hated the way she was thirty-three years old and so out of control of the way her body responded to anger. She should have better control over her emotions, just like the Bryn Ridge linguistics department director had warned her all those years ago. If you can’t even stop yourself from crying, maybe you’re not ready to be in this program…


“Maggie,” Arthur said tentatively, but she didn’t turn around. She heard the wheels of his desk chair scoot closer to her.


“I know what people—what men—think of women who cry at work,” she mumbled. “I know this is unprofessional.”


Arthur touched her shoulder gently, turning her around to face him. “The only person who was unprofessional here was the one who was so checked out of his work that your program suffered. I don’t even remember half of those budget meetings,” he admitted. He reached his fingers up, almost like he was going to graze her cheek and wipe a tear away, but he must have thought better of it. He tucked his palm underneath his leg. “Is this why you asked for eight thousand dollars when we made our bargain?”


“Obviously,” she answered with a hollow laugh. “This year, I was going to work on my own translation of Branagh’s Aubade, so it probably stung quite a bit more than it would have any other year.”


“I wish you had told me,” Taliesin said, but then he added, “I wish I had been paying attention in those damn committee meetings.”


“I thought…” Maggie chewed on her words, trying to figure out whether he had earned any vulnerability from her. “I thought you didn’t think the program was worthwhile.”


He made a small sound, but she couldn’t quite tell what it was. Exasperation or frustration. “You’re getting the money you asked for. I don’t care if you stop helping me right now. I’ll fix this. You and your students can take the trip in the fall.”


She smiled at him sadly. “Even with the money from the bargain, it will be too late for the fall. Students won’t have had a chance to sign up.”


“Then you’ll just have to go in the spring. If I have to plan your trip to Branagh’s yew field myself, I will. I’ll go to Dean Clearwater right now and get it sorted,” he said, standing up.


“No!” Maggie nearly shouted. That was the last thing she needed, for the dean to think she had done something to get Arthur Taliesin to put in special budgetary requests for her. “Dean Clearwater will think I blackmailed you or something.”


He smirked. “Or something.”


“Please,” she said. “Don’t go to the dean. It wouldn’t go well for me. We’ll figure it out after the pall is taken care of.”


Heat bloomed on her cheeks as her anger unspooled, but she still felt better with the desk between them, with the fizzing dregs of her anger still in the air. “As long as we clear this pall by next spring, I suppose I could make the seminar work,” she said.


“Above and below, if this thing isn’t gone by July, I’m going to be the one crying in this office.” He watched her expression carefully, as if to make sure she was okay with the crying comment, and she rewarded him with a small smile. His own grin widened, but only for a moment before it fell and his furrow was back. “I’m sorry. This year has been hard, and even before the pall fell, I haven’t been focused. I thought coming to Hawthorn would…oh, I don’t know, reinvigorate something that I lost at Dartwood. But I’m still a little lost. And people keep getting hurt because of it.”


Maggie wasn’t sure how to ease this for him. More, she wasn’t sure she wanted to. There was some truth to the statement, after all. “I hope you find what you’re looking for,” she finally said.


Taliesin’s gaze was distant for a moment before he replied, “Me, too.” With a small shake of his head, he seemed to cast off whatever feeling or memory he had gotten lost in. He looked up at the ancient clock that sat above a curling poster for the student-run literary magazine and sighed, testing the limits of his too-small desk chair by leaning back. He took off his glasses and rubbed his eyes. “I still have to enter a few more grades before the end of the day.”


“You better get to it, or Edna will have something to say about it,” she said, and she almost sounded like her normal self.

facts.fact: Rory 短信催战：计划一周没进展——不用校园中央亲热，做点什么。
天意：她发间粘着山楂花瓣——他拂开擦过耳垂，半念头神意。
grow lights 政策：说服院长给一英里内居民免费发放；私心是请她拿两盏回家放阳台。
Annex 描写：银页岩/苔藓/茅草顶/faerie cottage 意象；Pearl Paige 见他紧张（Rowena 之子的老毛病）。
facts.anchor: faerie cottages from the old Diadhan poems

facts.fact: 地图证据：建庄园前 30 年起至少六次修路穿 Wilds——工地被 fantasmia 淹、土地反抗驯服。
facts.anchor: attempted to build a road through the Wilds

facts.fact: 反馈环假说：ghoul/wraith 群的能量喂养 pall（她的怪物经济学）。
Wheatly 日志：三河穿林、怪藤只攀河桦——他脱口 What if there was a convergence?。
facts.anchor: What if there was a convergence?

facts.fact: 星象实证：5 月 6 日（pall 落地日）月与双行星连珠 36 小时，峰值恰在 3:54 p.m.。
占运背刺：本季在不寻常之处迎接爱的可能——星星也推她向 Taliesin；她强力划掉。
facts.anchor: open yourself to the possibility of love

facts.fact: 8000 刀对质：不是百分比是全部（四年级翻译研讨课全程预算含实地考察）；他 Mine 她 Yours。
facts.anchor: isn’t a percentage; it’s the entire thing

facts.fact: 她的眼泪+Bryn Ridge 判词重播：33 岁控不住身体的怒反应；他把判词退还给该负责的人。
他的补救与自白：要立刻重排实地考察（被她急拦）；来 Hawthorn 想找回 Dartwood 弄丢的——还是有点迷路。
